questions.stem: Which article of the Indian Constitution establishes the Supreme Court of India?
questions.explanation: **Article 124** establishes the Supreme Court of India. Articles 124–147 collectively deal with the composition, jurisdiction, and powers of the Supreme Court.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Judicial review in India refers to the power of courts to:
options: Examine the constitutional validity of laws and executive actions
Advise the President on pending bills
questions.explanation: **Judicial review** is the power of constitutional courts to examine whether laws and executive actions conform to the Constitution and to declare them void if they do not. It is a cornerstone of India's constitutional governance.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Which writ is issued to produce a person who has been illegally detained before a court of law?
questions.explanation: **Habeas Corpus** (Latin: 'you may have the body') is a writ commanding that a detained person be brought before a judge to determine the legality of detention. It is a bulwark against arbitrary imprisonment.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The Supreme Court of India held its first sitting on which date?
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court of India was constituted under the new Constitution and held its **first sitting on 28 January 1950**, two days after India became a Republic on 26 January 1950. It replaced the Federal Court of India.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The writ of 'Mandamus' is issued by a court to:
options: Direct a public authority to perform a mandatory legal duty
Prohibit an inferior court from exceeding its jurisdiction
Produce a detained person before the court
Challenge the authority of a person holding public office
questions.explanation: **Mandamus** (Latin: 'we command') is a writ commanding a public authority, government official, lower court, or any legal body to perform a duty that is purely ministerial and required by law.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Under Article 21 of the Indian Constitution, the right to life and personal liberty can be restricted only by:
options: An executive order of the President
A simple majority resolution in Parliament
questions.explanation: Article 21 states that no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to **procedure established by law**. The Supreme Court in Maneka Gandhi (1978) held that such procedure must also be just, fair, and reasonable.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court of India under Article 131 covers disputes between:
options: Two private companies disputing a contract
The Supreme Court and High Courts on procedure
The Union and one or more States, or between two or more States
A citizen and the Central government over tax matters
questions.explanation: Article 131 grants the Supreme Court **exclusive original jurisdiction** over disputes involving (a) the Union and one or more States, or (b) the Union and States on one side and one or more States on the other, or (c) two or more States among themselves.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Which writ literally means 'by what authority?' and is used to challenge whether a person has the right to hold a public office?
questions.explanation: **Quo Warranto** (Latin: 'by what authority?') challenges a person's right to hold a public office. If the court finds the person is not legally entitled to the position, it can order removal.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The doctrine of the 'basic structure' of the Indian Constitution was enunciated by the Supreme Court in which landmark case?
options: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980)
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
questions.explanation: The **Kesavananda Bharati case (1973)** — a 13-judge bench ruling — established that Parliament cannot amend the 'basic structure' of the Constitution. Fundamental features (supremacy of the Constitution, democratic republic, secular character, separation of powers) are protected.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Judges of the Supreme Court of India are appointed by:
options: The Chief Justice of India alone
questions.explanation: Under Article 124(2), judges of the Supreme Court are appointed by the **President of India** after consultation with the Chief Justice of India and other judges as prescribed. In practice, the collegium system drives recommendations.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The retirement age of judges of the High Courts is:
questions.explanation: Under Article 217, High Court judges retire at the age of **62 years**. Supreme Court judges retire at 65 years (Article 124).
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The writ of 'Certiorari' is issued by a superior court to:
options: Order a public body to perform its duty
Restrict an inferior court from proceeding further
Quash the record of a lower court to correct legal errors
questions.explanation: **Certiorari** (Latin: 'to be certified') is issued to call up and quash the records of a lower court or tribunal where there has been an error of jurisdiction or a violation of natural justice. It goes one step further than Prohibition (which prevents; Certiorari corrects).
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Public Interest Litigation (PIL) in India was primarily made accessible through:
options: Relaxation of locus standi (standing) by the Supreme Court through judicial activism
An amendment to the Code of Civil Procedure
questions.explanation: PIL developed through **judicial activism by the Supreme Court**, particularly under Justice P.N. Bhagwati and Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer in the 1970s–80s. The Court relaxed the traditional 'locus standi' rule, allowing any public-spirited person to file a petition on behalf of those unable to do so themselves.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: For appointment of a judge to the Supreme Court, the collegium consists of how many members?
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court **collegium for recommending SC judge appointments** consists of the Chief Justice of India (CJI) and the **4 senior-most judges** of the SC = **5 members** in total. For HC judge appointments, the collegium has 3 members (CJI + 2 senior judges).
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Under which article can a citizen approach the High Court for issuance of writs for purposes beyond merely enforcing Fundamental Rights (i.e., broader writ jurisdiction)?
questions.explanation: **Article 226** empowers High Courts to issue writs for enforcement of Fundamental Rights AND 'for any other purpose'. In contrast, Article 32 applies to the Supreme Court for Fundamental Rights only. Article 226 is thus broader in scope.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the five constitutional writs that can be issued under Articles 32 and 226?
questions.explanation: The five constitutional writs are: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo Warranto. An **Injunction** is a remedy granted by civil courts under the Specific Relief Act and is NOT a constitutional writ.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Judicial activism in India primarily refers to:
options: Courts interpreting the Constitution broadly to protect rights and fill gaps left by the legislature and executive
Judges actively participating in parliamentary debates
Courts replacing the executive in day-to-day governance
Judges conducting public hearings in rural areas
questions.explanation: **Judicial activism** describes a tendency of judges to interpret the Constitution broadly and creatively — expanding rights, issuing directions to executive agencies, and filling policy gaps — rather than restricting themselves strictly to the text of laws.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Under which article does the Supreme Court have power to transfer cases from one High Court to another?
questions.explanation: **Article 139A** empowers the Supreme Court to transfer cases involving substantially the same questions of law either to itself or from one High Court to another, ensuring uniform interpretation of law across the country.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Lok Adalats established under the Legal Services Authorities Act have the legal status of:
questions.explanation: Under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, Lok Adalats are deemed to be **civil courts**. Their awards (settlements) are final, binding, and executable as decrees of civil courts — and are not subject to appeal in any court.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) was formally constituted in the year:
questions.explanation: NALSA was constituted under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, and formally operationalized on **9 November 1995**. Its mandate is to provide free and competent legal services to weaker sections of society.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The Supreme Court's 'special leave petition' (SLP) jurisdiction under Article 136 allows it to:
options: Hear appeals from any court or tribunal in India at its discretion (with constitutional exclusions for military tribunals)
Hear only criminal appeal cases from High Courts
Review administrative decisions of Union ministries
Issue advisory opinions to the President on constitutional questions
questions.explanation: **Article 136** is the residuary appellate jurisdiction of the SC. It grants discretionary power to grant special leave to appeal from any judgment of any court or tribunal in India (except courts/tribunals constituted by law relating to armed forces). It is a 'leave' — the SC can refuse to admit the petition.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: In which landmark case did a 9-judge bench of the Supreme Court unanimously rule that the right to privacy is a fundamental right under the Indian Constitution?
options: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017)
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
questions.explanation: In **Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017)**, a 9-judge constitutional bench unanimously held that the right to privacy is a fundamental right protected under Articles 14, 19, and 21 of the Constitution.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: A judge of the Supreme Court can be removed from office by:
options: The President on the advice of the Prime Minister alone
The Chief Justice of India on grounds of proven misbehaviour
An address by each House of Parliament passed by a special majority (majority of total members + 2/3 of members present and voting)
A simple majority resolution passed by Parliament
questions.explanation: Under Article 124(4), a SC judge may be removed by the President only after **each House of Parliament passes an address** by a majority of its total membership AND a majority of not less than **2/3 of members present and voting**. This stringent process protects judicial independence.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 143 refers to:
options: The SC's power to give legal advice to ordinary citizens
The SC advising the CJI on collegium recommendations
The SC auditing government accounts on request
The President's power to refer questions of law or fact of public importance to the SC for its opinion
questions.explanation: **Article 143** empowers the **President** to refer any question of law or fact of public importance to the Supreme Court for its opinion. The SC may give or may decline to give its opinion. This opinion is advisory — not binding — but has high constitutional weight.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The principle of 'separation of powers' in India, as compared to the USA, is best described as:
options: Explicitly codified in all three branches of the Constitution
Equally and rigidly applicable at both Union and State levels
Not rigidly applied but implied through distinct constitutional provisions for each organ, with checks and balances
Applicable only to the judiciary, not to the legislature or executive
questions.explanation: India does not rigidly separate powers as the US Constitution does. The Constitution does **not** use the term 'separation of powers' explicitly. However, distinct constitutional provisions for Legislature (Part V, Ch II), Executive (Part V, Ch I), and Judiciary (Part V, Ch IV) along with checks and balances imply a functional separation without rigid compartmentalization.
questions.subject: Polity
